title: AI Pentest Cost vs Manual Pentest: 2026 Prices Compared
summary: Published 2026 prices for AI pentests ($50 per task-hour to $10,000 per app) vs manual tests ($5K to $30K+), with retest terms and billing models.
body_markdown:
An[AI penetration test](https://codeant.ai/pentesting) in 2026 costs from $50 per agent task-hour (AWS's own example of a 4-hour routine test comes to $1,200) to $10,000 per web app per test, and most published per-test prices sit between $3,500 and $5,085. A manual pentest of one web app usually costs $5,000 to $30,000, with senior testers billed at $1,200 to $3,000 a day. CodeAnt AI fits security and engineering leads who need an exploit-proven pentest and a SOC 2 and ISO 27001-ready[report within 48 hours](https://codeant.ai/blogs/pentesting-vendors) , and who want to test every quarter instead of once a year.


CodeAnt AI has run 12,000 pentests and is trusted by more than 1,000 companies, including Fortune 500 companies like NRG, cybersecurity leaders like Commvault, and fast-growing companies like 11x and Sanas.


The sticker price is rarely the full bill. What you pay for depends on the pricing model: tester hours, tests, credits, agent task-hours or results. This guide compares the prices eight AI pentest providers publish, each checked on the provider's own page on November 4, 2026, next to published market ranges for manual testing. It then covers what each pricing model charges you for, where AI testing beats a human tester and where it does not, and how to work out what a year of testing costs your team.

## What Are You Paying For When You Buy an "AI Pentest"?


Three different products are sold under the same name, and they are priced differently because they deliver different things.


-


Scanners with an AI label. They find candidate issues and rank them, but they do not prove that an attacker can use them. Cheap, fast and noisy. Not a pentest.


-


Human-led pentests with AI assistance. A consultant runs the test and uses AI tools to go faster. You still pay for consultant time, and the test still happens once or twice a year.


-


Autonomous AI pentests with human validation. Agents map the attack surface, chain issues together and try to prove each one with a working exploit; a security researcher reviews the result before it reaches you. This is the category[Cobalt](https://codeant.ai/blogs/codeant-ai-vs-cobalt) 's Autonomous Pentest,[Synack](https://codeant.ai/blogs/codeant-ai-vs-synack) 's Sara and CodeAnt AI sell.[Intruder](https://codeant.ai/blogs/codeant-ai-vs-intruder) and[Aikido](https://codeant.ai/blogs/codeant-ai-vs-aikido-security) sell AI pentests too, and how much human review each vendor includes differs.


Ask any vendor two questions before comparing prices: does every finding come with proof that it can be exploited, and does a person check the findings before you see them?

The same guide puts most engagements at $10,000 to $30,000, specialist researchers at $150 to $400 an hour and senior testers at boutique firms at $1,200 to $3,000 a day.


[Manual tests](https://codeant.ai/blogs/why-manual-penetration-testing-is-not-enough) cost this much because the price is built from hours. The vendor counts your assets (domains, IP addresses, endpoints, user roles), estimates hours per asset, multiplies by a rate, and quotes retests as more hours. On our calls, buyers running mostly managed cloud services say this breaks down: there are no fixed IP addresses to count, so every quote starts with a scoping argument.


## What Does Each Pricing Model Actually Charge You For?


The price on the page tells you less than the model behind it. There are five models in the market today.


-


Tester hours (most manual consultancies). You pay for the time spent, whether or not a high or critical issue is found. A retest is more hours.


-


Per test (Intruder, Cobalt's offer price, Synack Sara, NodeZero WebApp Flex). A fixed price per run, the same whether the test finds a lot or nothing. Check what one test covers: a standard Sara test covers up to 25 unauthenticated web apps or 100 host IP addresses, external only.


-


Credits (Cobalt packages, Synack, Aikido). You prepay and spend credits per test. A Cobalt credit is 8 hours of testing and does not roll over to the next contract year; Synack credits expire a year after purchase.


-


Usage (AWS Security Agent, XBOW). You pay for agent time. AWS counts task-hours across all agents running at once, so billable hours often exceed the time the test takes.


-


Outcome conditions (Aikido). Aikido waives the credits if a first, fully set-up test of 8,000 credits or less finds nothing high or critical. Retests and later runs are not covered.


Four questions to put to every vendor, in writing:


1.


What do I pay if you find nothing high or critical?


2.


How many retests are included, for how long, and what does one more cost?


3.


Does this price include the report my auditor or my customer will ask for?


4.


What scope does one test cover, and what makes a quote go up?


This is where[CodeAnt's model](https://codeant.ai/pentesting) is different: its pentesting is priced on the outcome, you pay only when a high or critical is confirmed exploitable with a PoC, and nothing when only low and medium issues are found, so the meter tracks real risk rather than time spent or seats provisioned.


## Is an AI Pentest as Good as a Manual Pentest?


It is better at some jobs and worse at others. The honest comparison:


Area


AI pentest with human validation


Manual pentest


Time to report


Hours to 2 days


Days to weeks; Synack lists 5-day and 14-day windows for its human-led tests


Breadth


Tests every reachable asset in one run


Limited by tester hours, so large scopes get sampled


How often you can test


After every major release or every quarter, because a run costs little to repeat


Usually once or twice a year


Business logic (approval flows, role abuse, multi-step workflows)


Good with a test account, but the logic still needs a human check


Stronger: OWASP's testing guide says automated tools find it hard to understand context


New attack ideas


Reuses known techniques at scale


Stronger on creative, one-off attack paths


Consistency


Two runs on the same target can find different things


Depends on the tester you get


Retesting a fix


Rerun the same attack on demand


Usually booked and billed as extra time


The useful question is not AI or human, but where the human sits. In the best AI pentests, agents do the breadth work and a researcher checks and deepens the findings. At CodeAnt AI, researchers confirm every critical finding before it reaches you.


A question buyers raise on our calls: can the AI find what a human tester finds in an approval workflow or an admin screen? The answer depends on access. A black-box test sees only what an outsider sees. With a low-privilege test account (grey box), the test can try every role and tenant boundary that account can reach, which is where broken access control, such as one customer reading another customer's data, shows up.


## What Does a Year of Pentesting Cost?


Compare a year, not a test. A simple way to build your number:


Annual cost = (tests per year x price per test) + (extra retests x retest price) + (internal hours for scoping, access, fixing and audit evidence x your hourly cost)

Why test more than once a year? A pattern we hear on calls: one full test in a quiet period, such as a code freeze before year end, then a retest a few months later. The retest checks only the original findings, so everything shipped in between goes untested until next year. The cost of missing something is not small: IBM's 2025 Cost of a Data Breach Report puts the global average breach at $4.44 million and the US average at $10.22 million.

## When Should You Pay for a Manual Pentest, an AI Pentest, or Both?


Pay for a human-led test when:


-


A regulator, framework or customer contract asks for a named human assessor or a specific certification on the report.


-


The application's risk sits in complex business logic, such as financial approvals or multi-party workflows, that needs judgment more than coverage.


-


You need a red team exercise that simulates a specific attacker over weeks.


An AI pentest fits when:


-


An audit, a customer security review or a release date needs a report within days.


-


You ship every week or two and want testing after major releases, not once a year.


-


You want every exposed domain, API and service tested, not a sample.


Many teams end up with both: AI pentests every quarter and after big releases, and a human-led deep dive once a year on the workflow that would hurt most if it broke.


## Build Your Own Number: the TCO Formula


The true cost is a formula, not a quote:


```text
Total   cost   =  base   pentest   fee
+  retesting   fees
+  (  developer   hours    ×   fully   loaded   rate  )
+  opportunity   cost   of   delays
```


```text
Total   cost   =  base   pentest   fee
+  retesting   fees
+  (  developer   hours    ×   fully   loaded   rate  )
+  opportunity   cost   of   delays
```


```text
Total   cost   =  base   pentest   fee
+  retesting   fees
+  (  developer   hours    ×   fully   loaded   rate  )
+  opportunity   cost   of   delays
```


Run it both ways with your own inputs. A representative manual year: $30k base, $10k retesting, $6k developer time (40 hours at $150), and a $50k opportunity cost from a two-week launch delay, for roughly $96k.


The continuous equivalent zeroes out retesting and the delay, drops developer time to a handful of hours, and leaves the platform cost plus any confirmed-exploit fees, a materially smaller number.


Fill in the four variables from your own last engagement (get three vendor quotes for the base fee, ask each about retest pricing, track the real hours your last pentest consumed, and use your finance team's loaded rate), and the right model usually becomes obvious.

## What Do Buyers Push Back On?


These are the pricing objections we hear most on calls, with straight answers.


-


"We already paid for this year's manual test." Keep it. Use an AI pentest on what has shipped since, or on the APIs your annual test did not cover, then compare results after your next manual test.


-


"The budget for this year is spent." Start with the one asset your auditor or customer is asking about. A single scoped test costs far less than a full program and gives you a report to show.


-


"Will my auditor accept an AI pentest?" Auditors judge the report, not the tool: scope, methodology, who did the testing, the date, the findings and proof of fixes. Ask your auditor before you buy, and ask the vendor for a sample report.


-


"How much of it is AI, and who checks it?" Ask every vendor this. At CodeAnt AI, agents do the testing and researchers confirm every critical finding before you see it.


## Bottom Line


A manual pentest buys tester time once or twice a year. An AI pentest buys coverage you can repeat. Published AI prices start well below a manual test, but compare a year of testing, ask what you pay when nothing serious is found, and check that the report is one your auditor will take.
